title: The Age of Emoji Is Here :D Do You Need a Translator?
excerpt: Can't we just talk like normal people? (´・ω・｀)
body:
Can't we just talk like normal people? (´・ω・｀)

Soon, 1.5 billion Windows users will be able to flip someone off online with a single tap.

According to [the latest emoji list from Emojipedia](http://blog.emojipedia.org/windows-10-emoji-changelog), the online encyclopedia of emoji, Microsoft will add a middle-finger emoji to Windows 10. That makes it the first tech company to let users "swear" in emoji within its interface.

![The middle-finger emoji coming to Windows 10](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121719d8ImY5nSTXvUiRD6.jpg-w600)

## A New Way to Interact

Besides the middle finger, Microsoft has decided that the little people in its new emoji set will be gray by default, and every one of them will come in six skin tones.

Microsoft is not the first company to take emoji seriously.

When Apple released iOS 8.3, it added [more than 300 new emoji](http://www.theguardian.com/technology/shortcuts/2015/feb/24/diverse-emoji-redhead-afro-beard-white-skin) in one go, including six skin tones for the little people. On the emoji keyboard, press and hold one of these aliens and you can find your own kind: skin color, hair color and sexual orientation can all be changed.

![Apple's expanded emoji with diverse skin tones](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160801183313xhtqnwK439PvajSV.jpg-w600)

![Choosing a skin tone on the iOS emoji keyboard](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121719eoMPOQ9laGV1cxU0.jpg-w600)

On the Apple Watch, beyond preset text replies and quick sketches, most basic communication may come down to emoji. You and your friends can send each other redrawn animated emoji. Apple has also applied its new Force Touch feature to emoji: press hard on the screen and you can change an animated emoji's color.

Google, for its part, has [released a keyboard for Android that recognizes emoji](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/8596.html). Instead of hunting for the emoji you want one by one, you just draw it.

Instagram already lets people use emoji as hashtags, and in a recent report it said that at least 40% of comments contain emoji.

The age of emoji has truly arrived.

Out in the wider world, emoji are printed on shirts, embroidered on shoes, [made into short films](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/8596.html), used to explain science, [turned into deals worth tens of millions of dollars](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/6181), and even entered as evidence in court. How did they come this far and become part of how we talk every day?

## First, There Was ":-)"

In the 1980s, the computer science department at Carnegie Mellon University made heavy use of "electronic bulletin boards" (online chat rooms, in other words).

When [Scott Fahlman](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~sef/sefSmiley.htm) proposed using ":-)" and ":-(" to tell serious messages apart from friendly jokes, he had no idea it would make him one of the 40 people who changed the internet. The original smiley grew out of that suggestion.

![Scott Fahlman, inventor of the smiley emoticon](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121720T7Ow45uNKSP0dz1B.jpg-w600)

According to records later recovered from backup tapes, the emoticon was born on [September 9, 1982](http://www.cs.cmu.edu/~sef/Orig-Smiley.htm).

As Professor Fahlman wrote [in his own account](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~sef/sefSmiley.htm), "It didn't seem like a big deal at the time."

![Fahlman's original 1982 bulletin-board post proposing :-)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021217207JqEYP3OLuDzTsXr.jpg-w600)

Looking back, it was a moment that changed the world. The emoticons that look like padding in published novels, and the XD, (*^__^*), :P and ( ^_^ )/~~ you still type now and then, all started here.

On any computer that supported ASCII, people could liven up a conversation with combinations of symbols and letters. In the years when picture messages were expensive to send, text art was what turned plain text messages into pictures.

People once worried that heavy use of emoticons would corrupt modern language. In fact they are nowhere near a threat: symbol emoticons such as LOL (laughing out loud) and OTL (a figure slumped on the ground in defeat) have not taken over the world's text boxes.

Fahlman has [said publicly that he doesn't like what emoticons have become](http://www.independent.co.uk/life-style/gadgets-and-tech/news/happy-30th-birthday-emoticon-8120158.html).

No matter. The little faces that have held their place in chat windows since the days of QQ, MSN and Fetion come from a different symbol system.

## 1995: Emoji Is Born on a Pager

In 1995, [The New York Times reported](http://www.nytimes.com/1995/04/10/news/10iht-bellcon.ttt.html) that if you stopped any high school girl on a Tokyo subway platform and asked whether she had a pager, the answer was always yes: everyone has one, and without it how would my friends reach me?

Emoji was born on what was then the most popular gadget among young Japanese. That is why the word we use for these symbols is not the English "pictograph" but "emoji," the romanized spelling of the Japanese word for "picture character."

In 1995, the Japanese carrier Nippon Telegraph & Telephone (NTT) launched a pager that could attach illustrations of various facial expressions, such as a heart, to a message. It won over young Japanese and took nearly 40% of the market. Only when a later model dropped the feature did NTT realize that these modest symbols were the "killer" feature that made teenagers buy its product.

To win back the market it had lost, NTT's team developed the earliest emoji on its i-mode platform.

![An early pager emoji set](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121721rLcHOWuY7Fhksn5B.jpg-w600)

This pager emoji hides an Easter egg

Between 1998 and 1999, while working at NTT, Shigetaka Kurita invented emoji, the original form of the emoji we use today.

In an interview with The Verge, he said his goal was to create a full set of 176 color emoji, each 12x12 pixels, covering the whole range of human expression.

Unlike emoticons, which try to imitate pictures with characters, what Kurita built was a true system of symbols. From the start, they were meant to sit in a sentence without looking out of place.

On chat programs such as OICQ, QQ and Yahoo! Messenger, these face-like symbols caught on fast and became standard equipment. You may remember QQ groups flooded screen after screen with custom emoticons. People added captions to stills from films and cartoons to make animated emoticons, some almost as long as today's short videos.

OICQ and MSN have since left the stage, but the emoji that accompanied them all along are still being updated.

![Kurita's first emoji set, drawn on a 12x12 grid](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121722prnRhUkSF2ay0Vtl.jpg-w600)

The first emoji were a set of 12x12 symbols

## The Golden Age of Emoji

During the awkward shift from feature phones to smartphones, people naturally sent few emoji from their phones: if the recipient's phone was a different model, the emoji you sent might arrive as a string of garbled characters.

On messaging software such as QQ, of course, emoticons never went out of fashion, just as on WeChat today a conversation can run on nothing but emoticons.

Now, in the hands of Microsoft, Android and Apple, emoji have grown arms and legs, been made lifelike, then flattened again, and been given skin, hair and even sexual orientation in every color.

In October 2010, emoji were added to the Unicode standard for the first time, which carried them beyond Japanese phone systems and out into the world. Before that, in 2009, Apple had partnered with SoftBank to enter the Japanese market and built emoji into its phones. An Apple intern at the time, [Willem Van Lancker](http://www.willemvanlancker.com/), designed a commercial emoji set for the purpose: nearly 500 emoji covering all kinds of everyday things.

In September 2010, [Apple added emoji to the official iOS 5 keyboard](http://9to5mac.com/2011/06/08/standard-emoji-keyboard-arrives-to-ios-5-heres-how-to-enable-it/), making it Apple's first mobile operating system with built-in emoji. Google didn't add emoji to its keyboard until 2013. Once emoji rode in on the iPhone, you have to admit, firing one off became much easier. Even businesspeople who guard their image closely can't resist sending an OK hand sign or two.

So much so that when Japan's three big wireless carriers announced a unified emoji system, it barely counted as news.

In August 2014, the online Oxford Dictionaries added "emoji" as an entry. After all those years, it had become a standard new word.

![The emoji keyboard in iOS](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121722yXSbQRNW0veP1wiY.jpg-w600)

*Apple adds emoji to its keyboard for the first time*

## Reading Pictures, Reading Emoji, Reading Emotions

Emoji have grown up alongside the smartphone. You can see this plainly in [a recent report from the photo-sharing network Instagram](http://instagram-engineering.tumblr.com/post/117889701472/emojineering-part-1-machine-learning-for-emoji).

![Chart of emoji use on Instagram over time](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/2016070212172325PSfcDRiEO3vt1M.jpg-w600)

*Source: Instagram*

The turning points in Instagram's rising emoji curve clearly line up with updates to the iOS and Android keyboards. By March 2015, more than half of all text on Instagram contained at least one emoji.

Instagram data engineer Thomas Dimson [wrote on the company's engineering blog](http://instagram-engineering.tumblr.com/post/117889701472/emojineering-part-1-machine-learning-for-emoji) that emoji are becoming an effective, almost universal form of expression. In Finland, the most enthusiastically "emoji-fied" country, emoji appear in as much as 60% of text.

This also has to do with what Instagram is. On a social network that encourages people to snap and post photos, users already lean toward pictures over words. They would rather post a photo of a sunrise than write, "The eastern sky turned the pale white of a fish's belly, and slowly, slowly, a red disc leapt from the sea."

Everyone is looking at pictures, and whether there's text barely matters. Now that even hashtags can be emoji, Instagram will only fill up with more of them.

Instagram, Snapchat and even WeChat Moments have become the breeding ground for emoji's conquest of the world. (WeChat contacts who use emoji as their usernames really do stand out.)

## An App Where You Can Only Chat in Emoji

At first people used emoji one at a time. Now some fanatics have started building whole sentences out of them.

If you can't read them, it just means you haven't learned the language yet. Last September, someone built [an app where you can only chat in emoji](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/2103.html): [emoji.ly](http://emoj.li/). Naturally it took off, and it is a real brain-teaser.

In the month when usernames were open for reservation, 70,000 people signed up. Keep in mind that a username can be made only of emoji, and whether you will remember your randomly assembled ID the next time you log in is anyone's guess.

On Emoji.ly, usernames and messages alike can contain only emoji. Don't bother pressing Enter; the thing doesn't even support spaces. Every conversation is one long guessing game.

![Screenshots of the Emoji.ly chat app](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121723yQDnHtAiI8k9socK.jpg-w600)

When emoji are the only way to communicate, understanding their grammar matters a great deal. Linguists who weren't ready to make emoji a subject of study may find that the time has come.

## The Emoji You Send Can Be Used Against You in Court

Earlier this year, Osiris Aristy, a teenager in Brooklyn, New York, was arrested on suspicion of terrorism. It all started with [a threatening message he posted on Facebook, followed by gun and police-officer emoji.](http://www.buzzfeed.com/nicolasmedinamora/how-a-post-911-law-can-get-you-arrested-for-your-emoji-choic#.fxE628LNQ)

![The Facebook post with gun and police emoji](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121723sZdo1WAH78D5U9tI.jpg-w600)

Over the past year, emoji have figured in the evidence and trials of several American cases. As *Wired* put it in its report on the trend: [Emoji matter](http://www.wired.com/2015/02/emoji-in-court-cases/).

## Emoji as Art

You may already have seen a series or two that remakes famous paintings in emoji.

Lately, Emojinalart on the blogging platform Tumblr has been posting a stream of animated artworks made from emoji.

Crude and simple, right? That is probably just the nature of emoji.

![An animated emoji artwork by Emojinalart](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021217243r8wuD25L6y97koi.gif-w600Gif)

## Writing a Book in Emoji

In 2009, Fred Benenson, a data engineer at Kickstarter, led a project to translate an entire book, *Moby Dick*, into emoji, under the title *[Emoji Dick](http://www.emojidick.com/)*. The book has about 10,000 sentences, each translated by three people, and more than 800 people spent a total of 3,795,980 seconds on it.

Last year, the US Library of Congress added the book to its permanent collection.

![Pages from Emoji Dick](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121725jb4G1hogtT8qenKp.jpg-w600)

In 2012, Fred was invited to design an emoji cover for *The New Yorker*. Now he has launched a new crowdfunding project on Kickstarter: [Emoji Translation](https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/fred/the-emoji-translation-project).

The project aims to raise US$15,000 to build an emoji translation engine through crowdsourcing.

![Sentences from the Emoji Translation Project](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121725EHTKafXIAvByDxmL.jpg-w600)

You can already run simple emoji searches on Bing. Longer sentences are easier to misread (just look at the ones above!). A standard translation does seem necessary.

## Explaining Science in Emoji

Bill Nye, the American educational TV host, has made a series of videos that explain scientific concepts with emoji instead of elaborate animation.

Topics include [holograms](http://www.salon.com/2015/05/04/watch_bill_nye_explain_how_holograms_work_only_with_emoji/) and what evolution is really about. He still uses some words to string the emoji together, and he never stops talking, but emoji turn out to explain how molecules bond, copy themselves and reproduce with surprising clarity.

![Bill Nye's emoji science video](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/2016070212172607oGjJeBLt5kbvyn.jpg-w600)

*In his latest video, Bill pays tribute to Star Wars with donut-shaped emoji*

## The State of the Union in Emoji

This January, when President Obama delivered his State of the Union address, The Guardian set up the Twitter account @emojibama and translated the speech into emoji (mostly; a few English words remained).

The paper explained the idea this way: "Obama urged Congress, 'this year, let's find the areas where we agree.' If there is one thing in the world we can all agree on, it is emoji."

Below is an excerpt. For the full text and the side-by-side version, [click here](http://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2015/jan/20/-sp-state-of-the-union-2015-address-obama-emoji).

![An excerpt of the State of the Union translated into emoji](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021217262bI8dW0jt9OPrcGa.jpg-w600)

Emoji won't destroy language. They have become an extension of it, and even language in their own right.

Unlike character emoticons, which take a moment of decoding, emoji icons get the meaning across faster than words: if you can transmit brainwaves directly, why bother writing slowly?

It's true that countless people use "Face with Tears of Joy," as the official description calls it, as a "crying face." But just as the same word means different things in different places, the fact that emoji get misread is what makes them more like part of a language.

## Your Emoji Say Who You Are

Like natural languages, emoji use reflects cultural differences. In April, the third-party keyboard SwiftKey [published a report](http://swiftkey.com/en/blog/americans-love-skulls-brazilians-love-cats-swiftkey-emoji-meanings-report/) that analyzed at least 1 billion pieces of data to chart how often emoji are used across 16 languages.

![SwiftKey chart of emoji use by language](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121727tLFgZkc6OYRGwBJu.jpg-w600)

*[Source: SwiftKey](http://swiftkey.com/en/blog/americans-love-skulls-brazilians-love-cats-swiftkey-emoji-meanings-report/)*

Overall, people use far more smiling faces than crying ones, and two of the five most-used emoji are about romance. Thank goodness: there is still love in this world.

SwiftKey also found that Canadians are especially fond of guns and money, and that Australians use alcohol and drug emoji at more than twice the world average. France is the exception to the smiley face's worldwide popularity: the French use hearts at a startling rate. Half of all the emoji they send are hearts, four times the global average.

QQ's *China Netizen Emoticon Report* suggests that China is the true emoticon superpower. In 2014, more than 90% of QQ's 800 million users used emoticons in their chats. QQ users sent more than 533.8 billion emoticons that year, and the most popular was still "Grin," which stands for a smile. "Picking Nose," a distinctly East Asian way of showing contempt, was also among the most used.

![Chart from Tencent's China Netizen Emoticon Report](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121727mvqwgfZBMstrx15G.jpg-w600)

*Source:* [*Tencent's* *China Netizen Emoticon Report*](http://isux.tencent.com/china-emoji-usage-report.html)

## Emoji Become a Business Worth Tens of Millions

In early February, the renowned type foundry Monotype Imaging [announced it would pay US$27 million](http://www.streetinsider.com/Management+Comments/Monotype+Imaging+(TYPE)+Announces+Acquisition+of+Swyft+Media+in+%2412M+%2B+Incentives+Deal/10215240.html) to acquire Swyft Media, a startup that specializes in chat emoticons. Founded in 2012, Swyft Media does one thing: it works with businesses to create themed emoticon packs for them.

Earlier this year, [a Business Intelligence report noted](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/6181) that by the end of 2014 there were nearly 2 billion users of mobile messaging apps worldwide, and predicted that by the end of 2015 that number would exceed the number of social media users. Using emoji to help express yourself has become a popular way of talking among young people.

Media coverage had already described Swyft Media as having "revolutionized the way advertising is delivered in mobile content." That is accurate. For users, emoticons are an important way to express their personality; for mobile messaging apps, emoticon packs have become a significant source of revenue; and for brands, this quiet, unobtrusive form of product placement is more efficient and cheaper.

Emoji have also become a way to build buzz before Disney films open. Ahead of the live-action *Cinderella*, [Disney made an emoji version of *Frozen*](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/7025.html): a short of about two and a half minutes that retells the film's entire plot as an emoji chat on a phone.

Brands such as Burger King, Taco Bell and Victoria's Secret have openly produced [whole emoji sets of their own](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/8566.html) that work seamlessly with popular Western social apps such as Facebook Messenger, WhatsApp and Path.

On WeChat, Xiaozaizi Theater, an emoticon label with a sizable following, [designed emoticons for McDonald's](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/4564.html) and has recently created a pack for a L'Oréal campus charity sale. Importing sticker packs into WeChat is tedious, but people keep doing it happily.

From brand-exclusive emoji to the more versatile stickers in messaging apps, people seem to need to type less and less.

![Brand emoji sets](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121728oKRGELc9fUsQ8m0q.jpg-w600)

## Emoticons Level Up: Cony, Moon, Sally and Friends

Line, the messaging app popular in Japan and Taiwan; KakaoTalk, popular in South Korea; and of course WeChat, which is well on its way to ruling the world, all have one thing in common: a huge range of stickers.

When it comes to stickers, LINE is the most successful. In the crowded messaging market, its rich cast of cartoon stickers is exactly what sets it apart, so much so that its staff sometimes can't tell whether they work for an internet company or a cartoon studio. [Its just-released results for the first quarter of 2015 show](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/9270.html) that its constantly refreshed sticker business is still one of its best-selling services.

By turning its cartoon characters into idols, LINE has shaped popular culture, especially in East Asia, where its success is tied to the spread of Japanese anime and manga culture (Japan is where emoji were born, too).

LINE users send [as many as 1 billion stickers a day](http://www.nytimes.com/2014/05/26/technology/no-time-to-text-apps-turn-to-stickers.html?_r=0), and in 2013 alone the company made US$590 million from them. [The top ten best-selling stickers averaged 4.7 million yen in sales](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/1516.html), and sticker purchases already account for 20% of Line's total revenue.

Beyond the official stickers, LINE Creators Market, a platform launched last April where users can upload and sell their own stickers, is also doing well, with 100,000 stickers so far.

Why are people drawn to Moon and Cony, and why do they pay for them? Probably because these cute, cheeky stickers convey feelings subtler than a greeting, a sweet nothing or a gripe. We once wrote a detailed piece on how Cony and friends took over the chat box; you can [read it here](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/780.html).

![LINE characters Cony, Brown, Moon and friends](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121728xTorSamw9V7dBvp5.jpg-w600)

When it comes to merchandise, LINE clearly knows best how to make money from its cartoon stickers. It developed [LINE Friends UT](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/189.html) with Uniqlo and [opened pop-up stores in Shanghai, New York and elsewhere](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/350.html). [Last Mid-Autumn Festival, the mooncake gift boxes LINE released in Hong Kong](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/1893.html) were so sought after that "a box was hard to come by." It makes the emoticon business look like easy money.

WeChat didn't add its sticker store until version 5.0 in 2013, but that hasn't stopped people from using emoticons on WeChat constantly. One QDaily editor runs a WeChat group that chats only in emoticons; drop in for a while now and then, and your saved haul will last a month of everyday chatting without a repeat. LINE is far ahead here, but WeChat, with its huge user base, is steadily building momentum in its sticker store.

Who hasn't suffered through a stretch of bone-dry chats after reinstalling WeChat?

## Emoticons Now Come With Plenty of Merchandise

If you really want to send someone a crying face, a cat face, a heart or a pile of poo, the comedian Nick Offerman suggests you put down your phone and try something more personal and old-fashioned: [how about a giant solid-wood emoji](http://www.cnet.com/news/chat-with-nick-offermans-handcrafted-wood-emojis/)?

Each physical emoji weighs 14 pounds (about 6.35 kilograms) and sells for US$29.99 (about 186 yuan). According to Offerman, you use them exactly as you would on a phone: just put one in the recipient's hands.

At normal usage rates, though, you might need a whole room to store your stock of "wooden emoji."

![Nick Offerman's handmade wooden emoji](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121729lkUYicS6M3xCDhNz.jpg-w600)

Betabrand, an online retailer of original designs, recently created [a shirt covered in poo prints](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/5997.html). Its crowdfunding campaign succeeded: 230 people pre-ordered, 3.6 times the target of 50 shirts. Betabrand founder Chris Lindland said the first run would be 800 shirts.

![Betabrand's poo-emoji shirt](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121729xmYPwAb52prOSiCy.jpg-w600)

These poo-covered shirts even look a bit businesslike. In fact, if you want to wear emoji today, whether on a T-shirt, a clutch, long johns or a skirt, you'll find plenty of designs.

The whole fashion world loves emoji. Or at least it did once, right?

## Can Emoji and Formal Occasions Coexist?

The world is a fun place, so don't take things too seriously. Still, our advice is that when you are truly serious about something, hold off on saying it in emoji. It's like ten years ago, when your boss would have told you not to put a smiley ":)" in a business email.

We don't object if you do it now, but we would still urge caution. [After all, whether grown men should use emoji at all](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/8136.html) is still hotly debated.

If one day Google Translate offers an option to translate emoji, don't be too surprised. Frankly, we could use it. How else would you turn an expense report you can't understand, and its emoji version you can't understand either, into the language of Muggles?

## Softer Than Words, a Lifeline for the Socially Anxious: Emoji

I've lost count of the times I've typed out a long message in the chat box, deleted it word by word, gone back and forth a few times, and finally sent something only slightly better than "heh": a smiley, or a grinning smiley.

Before language was born, humans who had just learned to walk upright may have had only facial expressions and gestures to communicate with.

When people wrote with pen and paper and had something to say, they walked over to the other person, looked them in the eye and said it.

Today we type everything on keyboards, and even face to face we reach for our phones as if by instinct: swiping left, swiping right, liking, tapping lightly at the keys, as though this were the comfortable way to communicate. Everyone keeps a little distance, faces blurred, like the icons on everyone's keyboard: besides faces showing every emotion, there are hands, animals, arrows, numbers and more.

We can't claim that one picture really can say what a whole article struggles to say. But the subtle feelings carried by emoji and stickers are another version of "all is said without a word."

We live in an age of mixed communication, in which reading pictures has also come to count as part of language. Or, put another way, modern people, spoiled by technology, are building a new language together. Calling it emoji seems too broad: besides emoji in the strict sense, this language should also include the growing number of stickers and custom GIFs on Line, WeChat and QQ.

In short: if you can look at a picture, why read the words; if you can send an emoticon, why type? This is a world conquered by emoticons. Have fun :)

![An animated emoji GIF](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121730wJdqebMzl1yfOSTR.gif-w600Gif)
